findings.source_passage: It was merely the condensation of the man. He was by no means ill-looking; quite the contrary.
findings.why_it_matters: The epigrammatic line 'merely the condensation of the man' is the rhetorical apex of the physical description paragraph; its loss flattens Melville's characteristic aphoristic compression and removes a critically noted phrase.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'It was merely the condensation of the man' after the description of Starbuck's thinness, before moving to 'His pure tight skin.'

findings.source_passage: A staid, steadfast man, whose life for the most part was a telling pantomime of action, and not a tame chapter of sounds.
findings.why_it_matters: This is a distinctive, critically noted formulation that characterizes Starbuck's entire moral economy through a memorable antithesis; its absence removes a voice-establishing and interpretively weighty phrase.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'a telling pantomime of action, and not a tame chapter of sounds' after the lingering-images-of-perils sentence.

findings.source_passage: courage was one of the great staple outfits of the ship, like her beef and her bread, and not to be foolishly wasted.
findings.why_it_matters: This concrete, ironic analogy (courage as ship's stores) is Melville's characteristically materialist register applied to an abstract virtue and adds interpretive texture to Starbuck's pragmatism.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the beef-and-bread simile in the paragraph on Starbuck's practical courage.

summary: The draft preserves all high-priority signatures—the democratic-God invocation, the 'I will have no man in my boat' quotation, the Bunyan/Cervantes/Jackson litany, and the valor-ruined-man passage—fully and often verbatim; three medium-or-lower losses (the 'condensation of the man' epigram, the 'pantomime of action' antithesis, and the beef-and-bread courage simile) are real compressions but do not individually rise to regeneration severity.
